topic.title: Homeostasis, insulin and diabetes
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: One of the most reliably examined topics in B1, worth 8 to 11 marks. Summer 2024 gave it Q8 at Foundation and Q3 at Higher — a blood-glucose graph, the reason for the delay after a meal, two ways insulin acts, and the long-term effects. March 2026 made it the paper's 6-mark QWC on both tiers: how blood glucose is lowered, why a person with Type 1 diabetes cannot do it, and how the condition is treated.
mustMemorise: Homeostasis: a constant internal environment so cells and enzymes work properly — limited here to blood glucose and osmoregulation
A hormone is a chemical messenger made by a gland, carried in the blood to a target organ
The pancreas monitors blood glucose constantly and releases insulin when it rises
Insulin's target organ is the liver: it absorbs glucose, then respires it or stores it as glycogen
Type 1: the pancreas stops producing insulin, early in life, insulin for life
Type 2: the pancreas gradually produces less, linked to lifestyle and obesity, diet first
Symptoms: high blood glucose, glucose in the urine, lethargy, thirst
Long-term effects: eye damage, kidney failure, heart disease, strokes
notOnThisSpec: Glucagon and the raising of blood glucose
Negative feedback as a named mechanism (the spec says it is not required)
The islets of Langerhans and the cell biology of insulin secretion
Insulin resistance at receptor level, and HbA1c testing
Temperature regulation as an example of homeostasis

The schemes reject answers that restate the question, so every 'how' answer needs an organ and an action; and 'any two from' lists carry the listing rule.

steps.working: The pancreas detects the rise in blood glucose concentration.
steps.decision: Start with the organ that monitors. The specification says the pancreas monitors glucose constantly, so it is the first marking point and it is easy to leave out.

steps.working: The pancreas releases insulin into the blood.
steps.decision: Name the hormone and say where it goes. A hormone is always released into the blood — that is what makes it a hormone rather than a nerve impulse.

steps.working: Insulin travels to its target organ, the liver, and causes it to absorb glucose from the blood.
steps.decision: This is the first of the two 'ways' CCEA asks for. Note which organ does the absorbing: the pancreas makes the insulin, the liver responds to it.

options: Because the liver is insulin's target organ
Because the pancreas cannot store glucose
Because the liver makes the insulin
whyMenu.explain: A hormone acts at its target organ. For insulin that organ is the liver.

steps.working: The liver cells respire the glucose, or convert it to glycogen and store it.
steps.decision: The second 'way', and the word that carries it is glycogen. Writing 'stores it as glucose' would be no change at all.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The pancreas constantly monitors the blood and detects the rise in glucose. It releases insulin into the blood, which carries it to its target organ, the liver. Insulin causes the liver to absorb glucose from the blood, and the liver cells either respire that glucose or convert it into glycogen and store it. The blood glucose concentration therefore falls.

accepted: it causes the liver to absorb glucose from the blood, and the liver cells convert that glucose into glycogen and store it

steps.working: Person B's pancreas does not produce insulin.
steps.decision: Start with the cause, not the symptom. Type 1 means the pancreas has stopped producing insulin altogether.

steps.working: So the liver is not made to absorb glucose from the blood.
steps.decision: Link the missing hormone to the organ that should have acted. This is the step that turns a fact into an explanation.

steps.working: The glucose is not converted to glycogen and stored, so it stays in the blood.
steps.decision: Finish with where the glucose ends up. The graph shows it never comes down, and this sentence says why.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) 16.5 mmol/dm³ at 90 minutes. (b) Person B's pancreas produces no insulin, so the liver is never made to absorb glucose from the blood and none of it is converted to glycogen and stored, so the glucose stays in the blood.

items.stem: Which organ monitors the blood glucose concentration and produces insulin?
items.skill: Separate the monitoring organ from the target organ

options.feedback: The pancreas monitors constantly and produces insulin when glucose rises.
The liver is insulin's target organ — it absorbs and stores the glucose. It does not make the insulin.
March 2026 examiners reported a few candidates naming the kidney here. The kidney filters the blood; the pancreas makes insulin.
The stomach digests food. The pancreas is the gland that monitors glucose.

items.stem: A question asks: 'Give two ways in which insulin lowers blood glucose concentration.' Which answer scores?
items.skill: Give the mechanism rather than restating the question

options.text: It makes the liver absorb glucose, and the liver converts it to glycogen for storage
options.feedback: Two actions, both with an organ and a change named. That is what 'how' means.

options.text: It lowers the blood glucose level and keeps it normal
options.feedback: That repeats the question. Summer 2024 examiners were explicit that answers largely repeating the question were not credited.

options.text: It is released by the pancreas and travels in the blood
options.feedback: True, but that is how insulin gets there, not how it lowers the glucose.

options.text: It turns glucose into fat and into protein
options.feedback: The specification names glycogen as the storage product in liver cells.

items.stem: What do liver cells convert the absorbed glucose into for storage?

options.feedback: Glycogen — the animal storage carbohydrate from §1.3.
Glucagon is a hormone; glycogen is the store. One letter apart, so write it slowly.
Starch is the plant store. Animals store glycogen.
Storing it as glucose would be no change at all — the point is that it is converted.

items.stem: Which statement about Type 2 diabetes is correct?

options.text: The pancreas gradually produces less insulin, and it is linked to lifestyle factors and obesity
options.feedback: Progressive, gradual, and lifestyle-linked — the specification's own wording.

options.text: The pancreas stops producing insulin, usually early in life
options.feedback: That is Type 1. Type 2 is a gradual reduction rather than a stop.

options.text: It is always treated with insulin injections from the start
options.feedback: In the early stages Type 2 can be controlled by diet; injections may be needed later.

options.text: It cannot be affected by diet at all
options.feedback: Diet is the first line of control for Type 2, which is one of the things that distinguishes it from Type 1.

items.stem: Which of these is a possible long-term effect of diabetes rather than a symptom?
items.skill: Separate the symptoms list from the long-term effects list

options.feedback: The long-term effects are eye damage, kidney failure, heart disease and strokes.
Thirst is one of the four symptoms, alongside high blood glucose, glucose in the urine and lethargy.
That is a symptom — and the easiest one to test for.
Lethargy is a symptom. The long-term effects are the damage done over years.

parts.stem: State what is meant by homeostasis.

accepted: keeping a constant internal environment so that cells and enzymes work properly

scheme.for: maintaining a constant internal environment
so that cells and enzymes function properly
accept: so enzymes work at their best

hints: Two halves: what is kept constant, and why it matters.
parts.workedSolution: Homeostasis is maintaining a constant internal environment so that cells and enzymes can function properly.

commonErrors.feedback: The first half is there. The second marking point is why it matters — cells and enzymes only work properly within a narrow range.

parts.stem: Give the two examples of homeostasis named in this specification.

accepted: controlling blood glucose concentration and osmoregulation

scheme.for: controlling blood glucose concentration
osmoregulation (water balance)

hints: The outcome says 'limited to' and then names exactly two.
parts.workedSolution: Controlling blood glucose concentration, and osmoregulation — controlling the water balance of the body.

commonErrors.feedback: Temperature control is homeostasis in general, but this specification limits the outcome to blood glucose and osmoregulation.

parts.stem:
A nurse tests a patient's urine sample.
Give one symptom of diabetes that this test can detect.

scheme.for: glucose (sugar) in the urine

hints: A urine test can only find what is in the urine.
parts.workedSolution: Glucose in the urine.

commonErrors.feedback: Those are the possible long-term effects of diabetes, not symptoms a urine test finds. The urine test detects glucose in the urine.

hints: The specification lists four symptoms; two of them are things the patient feels.
parts.workedSolution: Feeling very thirsty (or lethargy — being unusually tired).

commonErrors.feedback: Those are the possible long-term effects. The symptoms the patient notices are thirst and lethargy.

parts.stem: State one possible long-term effect of diabetes.

scheme.for: eye damage / kidney failure / heart disease / strokes

parts.stem: Describe what goes wrong with the pancreas in Type 1 diabetes and in Type 2 diabetes.

accepted: in Type 1 the pancreas stops producing insulin; in Type 2 it gradually produces less insulin

scheme.for: Type 1: the pancreas stops producing insulin
Type 2: the pancreas gradually produces less insulin
scheme.examinerNote: Both types must be described; one side alone is not a comparison.

hints: One stops, one slows. Say both.
parts.workedSolution: In Type 1 diabetes the pancreas stops producing insulin altogether. In Type 2 diabetes the pancreas gradually produces less insulin, and the condition is progressive.

commonErrors.feedback: The two are swapped. Type 1 is a stop, usually early in life; Type 2 is a gradual decline linked to lifestyle.

parts.stem: Give one way in which the treatment of Type 2 diabetes usually differs from the treatment of Type 1.

accepted: Type 2 can be controlled by diet at first, while Type 1 needs insulin as medication from the start

scheme.for: Type 2 can be controlled by diet in the early stages, whereas Type 1 requires insulin as medication throughout life
accept: Type 1 needs insulin injections from the start

hints: One of the two can be managed without medication at first.
parts.workedSolution: Type 2 can be controlled by diet in its early stages, whereas Type 1 requires insulin as medication throughout life.

parts.stem: Give two lifestyle factors linked to Type 2 diabetes.

accepted: obesity and a diet high in sugar

scheme.for: any two from: obesity / a diet high in sugar or processed food / lack of physical activity — [1] each

hints: The specification names obesity explicitly; the others follow from it.
parts.workedSolution: Obesity and a diet high in sugar (or a lack of physical activity).

parts.workedSolution: The pancreas constantly monitors the concentration of glucose in the blood. After a meal the concentration rises, and the pancreas responds by releasing insulin into the blood. The blood carries the insulin to its target organ, the liver. Insulin causes the liver to absorb glucose from the blood, and the liver cells then either respire that glucose or convert it into glycogen, which they store. The blood glucose concentration therefore falls back to normal. In Type 1 diabetes the pancreas has stopped producing insulin, so the liver is never made to absorb the glucose and the concentration stays high. The condition is treated by taking insulin as medication throughout life.

commonErrors.feedback: Insulin is made by the pancreas. March 2026 examiners reported candidates confused about the site of insulin production, a few naming the kidney.

findTheMistake.stem:
Sorcha is asked: 'Give two ways in which insulin lowers the blood glucose concentration. [2]'

findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Neither line says **how**. The question has already told her that insulin lowers blood glucose; the marks are for the mechanism — which organ insulin acts on, and what that organ does with the glucose.
correction: Insulin causes the liver to absorb glucose from the blood.
The liver cells convert the glucose into glycogen and store it, or respire it.

Summer 2024's report names this exactly: examiners were disappointed at answers that largely repeated the question.
